newsitem.title: USA: Beating back the debt burden.
newsitem.headline: Beating back the debt burden.

text.p: If I owe you $100, it's my problem. If I owe you $1 million, it's your problem.
Someday soon, the U.S. banking industry may have a problem with the enormous credit card debt that's out there. After all, personal bankruptcies are at record levels.
But for now, the growth in consumer debt is our problem and we're falling behind.
The American Bankers Association reported that a record number of credit card accounts -- almost four in every 100 -- were delinquent at the end of last year.

So far, this is not a problem at all for the banks and other issuers, who are reaping huge gains not just from their prompt payers, but getting fat on late fees and punitive interest rates charged their delinquent-but-not-defaulting customers.
No wonder they are sending out some two billion letters a year exhorting Americans to take new cards, according to figures from the Consumer Federation of America.
That's better than seven letters a year for every man, woman and child in the country, and I know I've gotten better than my fair share. (So also, now that I think about it, have my kids.)

When you add car loans, mortgages, home equity loans, car leases, student loans and personal lines of credit to the credit card totals, there aren't many Americans who don't get at least a little nervous when they think about their debts.
What you do about it depends on your personal debt level, your ability to manage those debts and the time you are willing to give over to running your credit life.

Despite new sales pitches, rebate offers, hidden fees and more from the credit card industry, the best consumer advice remains the same old story: Live beneath your means, pay your bills on time and incur no interest on consumable items.
Here's a brief rundown on how different types of consumers can manage their debts best.

-- You have a serious problem with debt if your payments (including your home mortgage) exceed 40 percent of the money you bring home; if you are only able to pay monthly minimums or cover the interest, if you find yourself taking advances from one card to pay another, if your balances are constantly growing rather than shrinking, and if your debt loads cause you to lose sleep, or occasionally, your lunch.

Attack your debts viciously. Leave all credit cards at home or freeze them in coffee cans so that you'll have to have a melt down to use them. Consider contacting the Consumer Credit Counselling Service (look in your local White Pages) and have them work out a payment plan for you. Consider extreme measures like extra jobs and yard sales to pay down this debt. Concentrate on making at least the minimum payments required to keep your credit rating clean.

-- You have a middling problem with debt if you never seem to pay off your cards, but think you should be able to. Lay your cards on the table and find the one with the highest interest rate. Dedicate as much extra money as you can swing every month to that card and pay minimums on the others. Don't use that card any more for charging purchases.

As that balance slips away, start dedicating those extra dollars to the next highest rate card. Avoid the rebate card trap of charging consumables just to get the rebates and then ending up financing them.
Adopt a policy of credit card use for emergencies only until your cards are paid off. Then start small to see if you have the discipline to be a convenience user.

-- If you pay no consumer interest, manipulate your rebate card use for your own gain and use your cards for convenience and emergencies, you probably don't have a debt problem. But don't relax just yet.
Read your card statements like a hawk: New fees keep creeping in, and nonrevolvers like yourself have the most to lose with some of the newest card rules.

For example, if you charge large amounts every month and only occasionally fail to pay them in full (say because you're travelling or simply write a check for the wrong amount) you can end up paying astronomically high interest charges on full two-month cycle balances.
That's a lot of interest for a small mistake.
Know all of the fees and benefits associated with the cards you have, only carry one or two with you, and remember to review often.
The higher the delinquencies go, the more the issuers will have to find fees and burdens for the rest of us to make all those letters worthwhile.
